date.label: Undated Judges narrative
date.note: Biblical narrative chronology is not independently established as an absolute BCE date.

claims.claim: The narrator condemns Gideon’s ephod as a snare to his household
claims.evidence: Judges 8:27 (Hebrew Bible, Judges 1–21, Masoretic text, read in full in Hebrew and JPS English via Mechon Mamre). Textual description only; the narrated event is not externally corroborated.

claims.claim: Gideon explicitly rejects being hereditary king while attributing rule to YHWH
claims.evidence: Judges 8:22–23 (Hebrew Bible, Judges 1–21, Masoretic text, read in full in Hebrew and JPS English via Mechon Mamre). Textual description only; the narrated event is not externally corroborated.

claims.claim: Judges 6:11 locates Gideon at Ophrah of the Abiezrites, but this precise ancient site has not been securely established by the examined evidence. Do not assign map coordinates as confirmed.
claims.evidence: Judges 6:11 (Hebrew Bible, Judges 1–21, Masoretic text, read in full in Hebrew and JPS English via Mechon Mamre). Qualified textual claim only; no external historical certification. Grounded by Niesiolowski-Spanò's peer-reviewed article (verified, pp. 478–479 read in full), whose opening sentence states the location of the biblical city of Ophrah is still unknown.

claims.claim: Judges 7 narrates Gideon’s force being reduced to three hundred in two stages — twenty-two thousand fearful depart, leaving ten thousand (7:3), and three hundred are selected at the water — followed by a night attack with trumpets, jars and torches that routs the Midianite camp, and the capture of the Midianite princes Oreb and Zeeb by the Ephraimites
claims.evidence: Judges 7:1–25 (Hebrew Bible, Judges 1–21, Masoretic text, read in full in Hebrew and JPS English via Mechon Mamre). Textual description only; the narrated event is not externally corroborated. The troop figures are narrative figures, not independently verified counts; no excavated battlefield for the rout is established by the examined evidence. The lapping manner (7:5–6) is a discussed detail, not a settled fact: Moody Stuart (verified, PEQ 27:4 (1895), p. 345, read in full) records the usual reading (drinking from the palm of the hand) and an alternative manner he reports observing; the claim does not decide between them, and does not use the lapping note to assert a military-selection rationale — the text's own stated reason is the one quoted from 7:2.

connections.note: Reluctant commission and divine reassurance (Exodus 3:11–12). This is a literary/thematic relation, not an independently verified shared historical event.
Priestly ephod context, not identity with Gideon's object (Exodus 28:6–12). This is a literary/thematic relation, not an independently verified shared historical event.
Debate about kingship and divine rule (1 Samuel 8:4–9). This is a literary/thematic relation, not an independently verified shared historical event.

review.notes: Proposed unpublished Judges category; source access remains limited and audit restrictions apply. Phase 4 readiness and independent QA are distinct. No editorial override needed: all 5 sources in sources[] are verified. S026 is not listed in sources[] — it is cited in the registry for the connections, but claims and connections carry no per-item source lists in the category JSON (J01/J02/J03/J04 precedent); the J05 draft cites no S026 footnote. JCL-05-003 is carried only with the registry's corrected wording (assessment unknown): Ophrah is unlocated and no map coordinates may be assigned as confirmed. JCL-05-004 is worded precisely: Judges 7 never states 32,000 — the claim gives the two-stage reduction (twenty-two thousand fearful depart, leaving ten thousand, 7:3; three hundred selected at the water). The draft's Judges 6:22 Class A guard note is stale — Phase 3 landed 2026-11-23 and the stored KJV text for Judges 6:22 now reads "O Lord GOD!" as the KJV has it; the guard note was not carried forward and the Overview's stale guard clause was removed. No internal research IDs (JCL-/JADD-) appear in the reader-facing prose.
